The most powerful refutation of Bentham’s felicific calculus is that it needs one summed total of the pleasures and pains of every consequence, including far-reaching and unforeseeable effects, while those consequences cannot be fully known and pleasures and pains lack one homogeneous, cardinally measurable quantity that intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent can add across persons. A method that cannot form that total cannot decide which act produces the greater balance of happiness.
